questions.question: In the generalized intermediate value theorem, what kind of function is $f$?
options: An arbitrary discontinuous function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$.
A function from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ only.
A continuous real-valued function $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$.
A function defined only on disconnected finite sets.

questions.question: What property of the set $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is assumed in the generalized theorem?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is finite.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is connected.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is empty.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is a singleton only.

questions.question: Let $f(\boldsymbol{a}) = 2$ and $f(\boldsymbol{b}) = 5$. Which value is between them and therefore covered by the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem under its assumptions?
For the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $f(x,y,z) = z$, what image is stated?
options: $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: What is the central meaning of the generalized intermediate value theorem?
options: A continuous function on any set attains a maximum.
A continuous function on a connected set cannot skip values.
Every function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has a maximum and a minimum.
Connected sets contain only one point.

questions.question: Which fact supports the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem at the level of images?
options: The continuous image of a connected set is connected.
The image of every set under every function is finite.
The image of a disconnected set is always connected.
The image of a connected set under any function is always a singleton.

questions.question: Let $f$ and $\boldsymbol{E}$ satisfy the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem, with $f(\boldsymbol{a}) = -1$ and $f(\boldsymbol{b}) = 4$. What can be concluded about $y = 0$?
options: There exists $\boldsymbol{c}\in\boldsymbol{E}$ such that $f(\boldsymbol{c}) = 0$.
No point in $\boldsymbol{E}$ can have value $0$.
The value $0$ is attained only at $\boldsymbol{a}$.
$\boldsymbol{c}$ must equal both $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$.

questions.question: For the closed unit disk in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $f(x,y) = x^2+y^2$, which image is stated?
Which assumption is essential for the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem to rule out skipped values?
options: Only that $\boldsymbol{E}$ has at least two points.
Only that $f$ is real-valued, with no continuity condition.
Connectedness of $\boldsymbol{E}$ together with continuity of $f$.
Only that $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$ are outside $\boldsymbol{E}$.

questions.question: How can the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem be proved when $\boldsymbol{E}$ is path-connected?
options: Compose $f$ with a path and apply the one-dimensional IVT.
Replace $f$ by a discontinuous function and use symmetry.
Use only the fact that $\boldsymbol{E}$ is finite.
Ignore paths and apply matrix multiplication.

questions.question: Assume the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem applies and $f(\boldsymbol{a}) = f(\boldsymbol{b}) = 7$. Which value is guaranteed to be attained between $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$?
A student applies the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem to a continuous $f$ on a set $\boldsymbol{E}$ but never checks whether $\boldsymbol{E}$ is connected. What is the problem?
options: The theorem needs the connectedness assumption on $E$.
Continuity alone always implies connectedness of $\boldsymbol{E}$.
The theorem requires $\boldsymbol{E}$ to be empty.
The theorem only works for complex-valued functions.

questions.question: Which property of $\boldsymbol{E}$ is required in the generalized intermediate value theorem?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is finite.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is empty.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is connected.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is unbounded.

questions.question: What kind of function appears in the generalized intermediate value theorem?
options: A discontinuous vector-valued function only.
A continuous real-valued function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$.
A function defined only on $\mathbb{N}$.
An arbitrary relation with no codomain.

questions.question: What does the generalized Intermediate Value Theorem say a continuous function on a connected set cannot do?
options: Take the same value twice.
Skip values between two attained values.
Have a compact image.
Be defined on more than one point.

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is continuous on connected $\boldsymbol{E}$, with $f(\boldsymbol a)=2$ and $f(\boldsymbol b)=6$. Which value must be attained?
options: Only $2$ and $6$

questions.question: Let $f$ be continuous on connected $\boldsymbol{E}$, and suppose $f(\boldsymbol a)=-3$ and $f(\boldsymbol b)=1$. Which conclusion follows?
options: There is no point with value $0$.
No point can have a negative value.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ must be disconnected.
There exists $\boldsymbol c\in\boldsymbol E$ such that $f(\boldsymbol c)=0$.

questions.question: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ on the closed unit disk, which value is in the image described?
options: $\dfrac12$
Every real number

questions.question: What role does connectedness play in the generalized intermediate value theorem?
options: It makes every function on the domain continuous automatically.
It forces all endpoint values of the function to be equal.
It prevents the continuous image from splitting into separated value ranges.
It makes the domain finite, so all values can be checked.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{E}$ be path-connected and $f:\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. If $f(\boldsymbol a)=1$ and $f(\boldsymbol b)=5$, why must some point have value $3$?
options: Because every path-connected set is finite.
Because $f$ must be linear on every path.
Because $3$ is the average of the coordinates of $\boldsymbol a$ and $\boldsymbol b$.
Compose $f$ with a path from $\boldsymbol a$ to $\boldsymbol b$ and apply the one-dimensional IVT.
